point_one.role: Show that pre-awakening is a staged physiological process rather than one precise internal alarm. Later-night sleep contains more light and REM sleep, while self-awakening experiments have found brain changes about 30 minutes before waking and heart-rate increases about three minutes before it.
point_one.new_listener_takeaway: A person may become progressively easier to wake and physiologically more prepared before opening their eyes, with different systems changing on different timescales. This offers a concrete explanation for waking near an alarm without claiming that the body has identified its exact ringing time.
point_one.evidence_anchor: F002 and F013 document the shift toward lighter and REM sleep later in the night and the greater sleep inertia associated with waking from deep N3 sleep; F005 reports right prefrontal and delta-power changes about 30 minutes before self-awakening, and F006 reports heart-rate increases beginning about three minutes before waking.
point_one.why_it_matters: It reframes the experience as a transition through a more wakeable sleep state followed by bodily activation, rather than as a mysterious all-or-nothing event. That helps explain why near-alarm waking can feel natural even when no exact time-reading mechanism has been demonstrated.
point_one.must_not_overlap_with_full_story: Do not repeat the Main Story’s general statement that the body may prepare before waking, its light-and-24-hour-entrainment explanation, or its cortisol findings from the 2025 home study. The Point should add the specific sleep-stage, brain-activity, and heart-rate timing rather than restating the broad conclusion.
point_one.must_not_overlap_with_other_point: Do not discuss whether repeated practice improves self-awakening or whether morning-type people are more likely to report it; those are the behavioral and individual-difference focus of Point Two.

point_two.role: Explain self-awakening as a partly learnable, person-specific pattern linked to repeated timing and chronotype, rather than a universal ability shared equally by everyone.
point_two.new_listener_takeaway: In a small week-long study, participants’ success reached 82% by the seventh day, while a separate university survey found that self-awakening reporters tended to keep schedules about 30 minutes earlier and show more morning-type tendencies. The practical insight is that a stable wake-time expectation may strengthen the pattern, especially for some individuals.
point_two.evidence_anchor: F007 reports an 82% seventh-day success rate after a week of attempting to wake at the usual time; F004 reports self-awakening in 66 of 643 university students, along with approximately 30-minute-earlier sleep and wake times and an association with morningness.
point_two.why_it_matters: This gives listeners a concrete reason why one person may regularly beat an alarm while another does not: the result may reflect learned timing and individual chronotype, not simply the strength of everyone’s circadian clock. It also suggests that consistency may make the experience more achievable, without promising precise or universal results.
point_two.must_not_overlap_with_full_story: Do not repeat the Main Story’s definition of self-awakening, its 17-study/715-person review, the ±30-minute success criterion, or its warning that participants generally knew the target time. The Point should focus on repeated practice, the seventh-day result, and the morningness association.
point_two.must_not_overlap_with_other_point: Do not explain sleep-stage changes, pre-awakening brain activity, or heart-rate timing; those physiological mechanisms and their different timescales belong to Point One.

【既に確定済みのMain Story本文(実際にこの内容が記事に使われます)】
The alarm has not rung. Then your eyes open. You check the time, and it is close to the time you were supposed to wake up.

This small morning surprise may be linked to the body’s own daily clock. Light helps set this clock. Regular times for sleeping and waking can also help keep it close to a 24-hour day.

In one laboratory study, healthy adults could follow a 24-hour schedule even under very weak light, when their rest and activity times were kept regular. The same setup usually did not make them follow a shorter 23.5-hour day or a longer 24.6-hour day.

Researchers also study a related event called self-awakening. This means waking near a planned time without an outside signal. A review found 17 studies with 715 people. But the studies were not all alike. Many counted waking within 30 minutes of the planned time as a success.

That makes the morning puzzle harder, not easier. Some experiments found changes in the body before people woke. But most participants knew the target time and were asked to wake then. So these studies show that people can sometimes prepare for a planned wake-up. They do not show that the body can read the exact time on an alarm clock.

A 2025 home study of 201 healthy adults adds another piece. On average, a body chemical called cortisol began rising about three hours before waking and reached its highest level about half an hour after waking. But the study found no clear faster rise during the final hour before waking. The people also differed greatly from one another.

So what happens when you wake just before the alarm? Your daily clock and your usual sleep schedule may help set the stage. The body may also begin preparing to wake before your eyes open. But research still describes this as a possible preparation, not a perfect inner alarm.
